screens.title: Encapsulation and Access Control
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on encapsulation: the practice of bundling data and the functions that operate on that data inside a class while restricting direct external access. Encapsulation prevents other parts of a program from putting objects into invalid states and makes maintenance safer. You'll learn the three access specifiers used in C++ — public, private, and protected — and how each one shapes what code outside a class can do. We'll show concrete examples, such as a sensor and a bank account, where getters and setters enforce validation, and we'll explain why const member functions let you safely call methods on immutable objects. We'll also cover the this pointer, which lets member functions refer to the object instance, and the limited, cautious use of friend functions and friend classes. By the end of this chapter you should be able to design a class that exposes a small, well-tested interface while hiding implementation details, recognize when encapsulation prevents bugs, and apply const and this correctly to make your intentions clear to the compiler and other developers. Consider how hiding implementation reduces accidental misuse: what public operations does your class really need?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to practical skills you will practice in this chapter. First, you will explain encapsulation and why separating interface from implementation reduces bugs in larger programs. This is not just a definition: you will point to concrete examples where hiding state prevents invalid updates. Second, you will master the three access specifiers — public, private, and protected — and know when each is appropriate. Third, you will implement getter and setter methods that validate input before changing internal state and understand how that validation enforces invariants. Fourth, you will use the this pointer and const member functions correctly so the compiler enforces your design intentions. Each objective ties to code examples and an assessment that asks you to refactor a BankAccount class. As you work, ask yourself: does each public method preserve the object's valid state? That question is the practical test of encapsulation.

screens.title: What is Encapsulation?
screens.narratorSegment: Encapsulation is the practice of grouping related data and the functions that act on that data into a single unit — a class — and controlling access to its internals. This is more than organization: it prevents external code from reaching in and corrupting an object by changing internal fields arbitrarily. A clear concrete example is a car: you have a small set of controls to operate it. You do not directly rewire the engine while driving. In C++, encapsulation is enforced with access specifiers that mark members as public, private, or protected. Public members form the object's interface; private members form the implementation that is hidden. One common misconception is that encapsulation only means making data private. Instead, it also means designing a coherent interface with operations that preserve class invariants — conditions that must always be true for the object. For example, if a class tracks a percentage, its setters should prevent values outside zero to one hundred. When you design a class, ask: which operations must be public for clients to use it sensibly, and which can remain private and replaced later without breaking users? That design question is the heart of encapsulation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is Encapsulation?
Encapsulation: a precise claim
Bundling of data and methods plus controlled access to implementation.
Why it matters
  • Prevents invalid state by centralizing validation in setters.
  • Allows changing implementation without breaking clients.
  • Improves reasoning about invariants and side effects.
Concrete analogy
A sealed device with knobs: knobs are the public interface; the sealed components are private implementation.
Common misconception
Making everything private is not sufficient; you also need a clear interface that preserves invariants.
Example: percentage holder
Keep the value private and expose setPercentage with validation to clamp or reject out-of-range values. Clients can read through a const getter but cannot write invalid numbers directly.
Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

Encapsulation is both hiding and designing a safe, minimal public interface that preserves invariants.

screens.title: public vs private vs protected
screens.narratorSegment: Access specifiers define visibility. Public members are part of the external interface and are accessible from anywhere. Private members are only accessible from within the class itself, hiding implementation details from all external code. Protected members act like private members for outside code but are accessible to derived classes; they are a bridge for inheritance that still hides members from general clients. A common pitfall is overusing protected to avoid writing proper accessors: protected leaks implementation to subclasses and can make future changes harder. Consider a Student class with a private grade and public setGrade and getGrade methods: the public interface ensures validation. Use public when you want clients to call the behavior directly, private when the detail should never be touched outside the class, and protected when derived classes must collaborate closely with the base implementation. When in doubt, prefer private plus explicit accessors over protected fields, because accessors allow validation and later refactoring without breaking derived classes. public vs private vs protected means public = external interface, private = class-only implementation, protected = class + subclasses.. In practical terms, who can access members and when to use each specifier. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Access Control
Access specifiers side-by-side
Compare who can read or modify members and typical uses.
public
Accessible from any code. Use for functions and data you intend clients to call or read.
Example: getGrade returns a safe read-only value.
private
Accessible only within the defining class. Use for implementation details like internal counters or raw state.
Example: a private grade member that only setters update with validation.
protected
Accessible within the class and derived classes. Use sparingly when inheritance needs tight cooperation.
Example: a base class caches a value accessed by subclasses.
Design guidance
  • Prefer private with accessors for validation and flexibility.
  • Use protected only when subclass behavior cannot be expressed through public APIs.
  • Avoid making everything public for convenience.
Key Takeaway
Choose the narrowest visibility that supports correct and maintainable code.

screens.title: Getters and Setters with Validation
screens.narratorSegment: Getters and setters are the standard way to provide controlled access to private data. A getter, often called an accessor, returns a copy or reference to internal state without changing it. Marking a getter as a const member function promises it will not modify the object and allows calls on const objects. A setter, or mutator, takes input and updates internal state after validating the input. The validation enforces invariants — for example, refusing to set a temperature below absolute zero or a negative account balance. A common mistake is to expose a non-const getter that cannot be called on const objects, or to implement a setter that blindly trusts the caller. In the visual code panel you will see a TemperatureSensor example with a const getter and a setter that rejects unrealistic values. Read the code to see how the setter prints an error message when validation fails. When you write setters, consider whether to clamp invalid values, reject them, or throw an exception; choose based on the class contract and expected usage. How will your setter preserve the class's invariant?

keyIdea.title: Accessors pattern
keyIdea.text: Getters should be const; setters validate input to keep objects in a valid state.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Getters & Setters
TemperatureSensor example
A const getter and a setter that rejects impossible temperatures enforce correctness.
// TemperatureSensor snippet for learning
class TemperatureSensor {
private:
  double currentTempCelsius;

public:
  TemperatureSensor(double initialTemp) : currentTempCelsius(initialTemp) {}

  // Getter declared const so it can be called on const objects
  double getTempCelsius() const {
    return currentTempCelsius;
  }

  // Setter validates input before updating
  void setTempCelsius(double newTemp) {
    if (newTemp >= -273.15) {
      currentTempCelsius = newTemp;
      std::cout << "Temperature updated" << std::endl;
    } else {
      std::cout << "Error: Temperature cannot be below absolute zero." << std::endl;
    }
  }
};
Explanation
  • getTempCelsius is const, so const objects can call it safely.
  • setTempCelsius enforces a domain check against absolute zero.
  • Validation keeps the sensor object in a meaningful state and prevents downstream errors.
Concrete scenario
When reading from multiple sensors, you may store const copies. Const getters allow you to read those copies without accidental mutation.
Check your understanding
Why would you prefer a setter that rejects invalid input over one that silently clamps values? Think about caller expectations and hidden side effects.

screens.title: Student class: private grade and validation
screens.narratorSegment: Let's ground encapsulation in a Student class example. The grade field should be private so external code cannot assign invalid values such as negative scores or values over one hundred. We provide a public setGrade method that checks the input and rejects or clamps it according to the class contract. A public getGrade method is declared const so callers can safely inspect the grade of const Student objects. One misconception is to expose the grade publicly for convenience; that makes it harder to enforce invariants and to change how the grade is stored later. In this example the setter prints an error when validation fails, but you could also choose to throw an exception or return a boolean. The key design decision is to ensure the public interface makes invalid states impossible or at least detectable. After you write the methods, test edge cases such as exactly zero, exactly one hundred, and values slightly outside. That test habit will reveal assumptions and lead to robust setters. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Student Example
Student class code
// Student grade example
class Student {
private:
  int grade; // stored privately

public:
  Student(int initGrade) : grade(initGrade) {}

  // Const getter
  int getGrade() const {
    return grade;
  }

  // Setter with validation
  void setGrade(int newGrade) {
    if (newGrade >= 0 && newGrade <= 100) {
      grade = newGrade;
      std::cout << "Grade updated" << std::endl;
    } else {
      std::cout << "Error: grade must be between 0 and 100." << std::endl;
    }
  }
};
Walkthrough
  • The grade field is private and cannot be written from outside.
  • getGrade is const, so it can be called on const Student objects.
  • setGrade enforces the 0–100 invariant, preventing invalid assignments.
Analogy: think of grade as a sealed gauge; only the setter updates it through a safe doorway that checks inputs.

screens.title: Using the this pointer
screens.narratorSegment: The this pointer is an implicit pointer available inside every non-static member function that points to the object on which the function was called. You rarely need to write this explicitly, but it becomes important when parameter names shadow data member names. For example, in a constructor that takes a parameter named balance, using this->balance clarifies that you mean the object's member, not the parameter variable. The this pointer is also used to return a reference to the current object from a method, enabling chaining, such as calling moveBy twice in succession. A misconception is to overuse this everywhere; that hurts readability. Use it when you need to disambiguate, when returning *this for chaining, or when taking the object's address. In our BankAccount activity you will intentionally write this->balance inside deposit and withdraw to practice explicit usage. Remember that within const member functions, this is a pointer to const, reinforcing the object's immutability in that context. Using the this pointer means use this to disambiguate member names and to return or reference the current object; prefer it only when needed.. In practical terms, referencing the current object and disambiguating names. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › The this pointer
Disambiguation example
// Point example using this
class Point {
private:
  int x, y;
public:
  Point(int x, int y) : x(x), y(y) {} // initializer list uses implicit names

  void setCoordinates(int x, int y) {
    this->x = x; // explicit this to avoid ambiguity
    this->y = y;
  }

  Point& moveBy(int dx, int dy) {
    x += dx;
    y += dy;
    return *this; // return reference to current object
  }
};
Notes
  • this is implicit; write it only when needed to clarify or return the object.
  • Returning *this permits method chaining; ensure you return by reference when appropriate.
  • In const methods, this has type pointer to const, preventing modification.
Practice: deliberately use this->member in two methods to get comfortable with the syntax and to show intent.

screens.title: Const member functions and const objects
screens.narratorSegment: Const correctness is the practice of marking member functions as const when they do not modify the object's non-static data members. Doing so communicates intent to other developers and allows objects declared as const to call those member functions safely. For instance, a getBalance method declared const can be called on a const BankAccount object; deposit cannot. A typical compilation error occurs when a const object attempts to call a non-const member function. This compiler enforcement is valuable: it prevents accidental state changes through code paths that were intended only to read data. One common misconception is that const is only about performance; it is primarily about correctness and clear contracts. In the lesson we will show a side-by-side comparison of calling a const getter and a non-const setter from a const object and explain the compilation failure. When designing classes, decide which methods form the read-only interface and mark them const. That small discipline leads to safer and more understandable code. Const member functions and const objects means mark read-only methods const to enable calls on const objects and to let the compiler enforce immutability.. In practical terms, why and how const prevents accidental modification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Const vs non-const call
// Example usage
const BankAccount savings("CONST001", 5000.0);

// Allowed: calling a const getter
// savings.getBalance(); // OK if getBalance is declared const

// Not allowed: calling a non-const setter
// savings.deposit(100.0); // Compilation error: cannot call non-const method on const object
Practical tips
  • Make simple getters const by default.
  • If a method logically does not change observable state, mark it const even if it modifies a cached internal value marked mutable.
  • Use compiler errors as guidance when refactoring: a const method contract lets you safely reason about callers.
Check: if a method only reads data and calls other const methods, declare it const so it can be used on const objects.

screens.title: Friend functions and friend classes
screens.narratorSegment: Friend functions and friend classes let specific non-member functions or entire classes access a class's private and protected members. They break the usual encapsulation barrier intentionally and are commonly used for operator overloading, such as implementing stream output where a non-member function needs to read private fields from two different objects. The justification for a friend should be narrow: performance or a natural non-member operation that logically belongs outside the class. A frequent design error is to overuse friend to avoid writing accessors; that choice often indicates the class boundaries are not well drawn. When using friend, document the reason and keep the friend scope small. An alternative is to provide carefully designed public accessors that give the friend the minimal information it needs while preserving encapsulation. In short, friend is a tool for specific problems, not a default pattern. Before making a function friend, ask whether a public getter, protected accessor, or redesign would maintain encapsulation better. Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Friend Declarations
When friends are used
A common, legitimate use is implementing a non-member stream insertion operator that needs access to private data from an object.
Alternative designs
  • Provide a minimal public accessor instead of making a function friend.
  • Reconsider class boundaries if many external operations need private state.
Cautionary note
Friend reduces encapsulation and can make maintenance harder; it should be a well-justified, documented exception.
Common mistake

Declaring many functions or whole classes as friends because creating one accessor seems tedious. That spreads internal knowledge and couples code unnecessarily.

screens.title: Designing a safe class: practical checklist
screens.narratorSegment: When designing a class, follow a short checklist to ensure proper encapsulation. First, list the responsibilities and decide which operations clients must perform; those become candidates for public methods. Second, identify internal representation details that may change and mark them private. Third, design getters and setters only when clients need read or write access; prefer getters to be const and setters to validate input. Fourth, avoid exposing internal containers directly; instead expose iterators or controlled views if necessary. Fifth, use protected sparingly; prefer private plus well-defined protected accessors when inheritance is required. Sixth, reserve friend declarations for narrowly scoped, documented cases like non-member operator overloads. Common pitfalls include exposing internal pointers or references that let callers mutate internal structures, and forgetting to mark read-only methods const. This checklist leads to classes that are easier to test, reason about, and evolve. After designing, write unit tests that try to break the invariants to validate your choices. Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › BankAccount Refactor
Starter code excerpt
// Key parts to implement
class BankAccount {
private:
  std::string accountNumber;
  double balance;

public:
  BankAccount(std::string accNum, double initialBalance) {
    this->accountNumber = accNum;
    this->balance = initialBalance;
  }

  std::string getAccountNumber() const { return this->accountNumber; }
  double getBalance() const { return this->balance; }

  void setBalance(double newBalance) {
    // Implement validation: reject negative balances
  }

  void deposit(double amount) {
    if (amount > 0) { this->balance += amount; }
  }

  void withdraw(double amount) {
    if (amount > 0 && this->balance >= amount) { this->balance -= amount; }
  }
};
Guided checklist
  1. Make accountNumber and balance private.
  2. Implement getAccountNumber and getBalance as const methods.
  3. Implement setBalance to reject negative values and print or return an error.
  4. Use this->balance in deposit and withdraw to practice explicit member reference.
  5. Create a const BankAccount in main and verify only const methods are callable.
Testing tip: write a unit that attempts to set a negative balance and asserts the operation failed so you know the setter protects invariants.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on encapsulation: the practice of bundling data and the functions that operate on that data inside a class while restricting direct external access. Encapsulation prevents other parts of a program from putting objects into invalid states and makes maintenance safer. You'll learn the three access specifiers used in C++ — public, private, and protected — and how each one shapes what code outside a class can do. We'll show concrete examples, such as a sensor and a bank account, where getters and setters enforce validation, and we'll explain why const member functions let you safely call methods on immutable objects. We'll also cover the this pointer, which lets member functions refer to the object instance, and the limited, cautious use of friend functions and friend classes. By the end of this chapter you should be able to design a class that exposes a small, well-tested interface while hiding implementation details, recognize when encapsulation prevents bugs, and apply const and this correctly to make your intentions clear to the compiler and other developers. Consider how hiding implementation reduces accidental misuse: what public operations does your class really need?

These learning objectives map to practical skills you will practice in this chapter. First, you will explain encapsulation and why separating interface from implementation reduces bugs in larger programs. This is not just a definition: you will point to concrete examples where hiding state prevents invalid updates. Second, you will master the three access specifiers — public, private, and protected — and know when each is appropriate. Third, you will implement getter and setter methods that validate input before changing internal state and understand how that validation enforces invariants. Fourth, you will use the this pointer and const member functions correctly so the compiler enforces your design intentions. Each objective ties to code examples and an assessment that asks you to refactor a BankAccount class. As you work, ask yourself: does each public method preserve the object's valid state? That question is the practical test of encapsulation.

These objectives expand into practical tasks you will perform. You will refactor a BankAccount class to make account number and balance private, implement const getters that can be called on const objects, and write a setter that rejects negative balances. You will deliberately use the this pointer inside member functions to reinforce when an identifier refers to a data member versus a parameter. Finally, you will learn when a friend function is acceptable — for example, when implementing a non-member stream output operator that needs to access private state — and why frequent use of friend hints at a design smell. These objectives focus on design reasoning: not only implementing features but also reflecting on whether a public method preserves the class invariant. By the end, you will be able to explain your design choices and identify safer alternatives.

Encapsulation is the practice of grouping related data and the functions that act on that data into a single unit — a class — and controlling access to its internals. This is more than organization: it prevents external code from reaching in and corrupting an object by changing internal fields arbitrarily. A clear concrete example is a car: you have a small set of controls to operate it. You do not directly rewire the engine while driving. In C++, encapsulation is enforced with access specifiers that mark members as public, private, or protected. Public members form the object's interface; private members form the implementation that is hidden. One common misconception is that encapsulation only means making data private. Instead, it also means designing a coherent interface with operations that preserve class invariants — conditions that must always be true for the object. For example, if a class tracks a percentage, its setters should prevent values outside zero to one hundred. When you design a class, ask: which operations must be public for clients to use it sensibly, and which can remain private and replaced later without breaking users? That design question is the heart of encapsulation.

Access specifiers define visibility. Public members are part of the external interface and are accessible from anywhere. Private members are only accessible from within the class itself, hiding implementation details from all external code. Protected members act like private members for outside code but are accessible to derived classes; they are a bridge for inheritance that still hides members from general clients. A common pitfall is overusing protected to avoid writing proper accessors: protected leaks implementation to subclasses and can make future changes harder. Consider a Student class with a private grade and public setGrade and getGrade methods: the public interface ensures validation. Use public when you want clients to call the behavior directly, private when the detail should never be touched outside the class, and protected when derived classes must collaborate closely with the base implementation. When in doubt, prefer private plus explicit accessors over protected fields, because accessors allow validation and later refactoring without breaking derived classes. public vs private vs protected means public = external interface, private = class-only implementation, protected = class + subclasses.. In practical terms, who can access members and when to use each specifier. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Getters and setters are the standard way to provide controlled access to private data. A getter, often called an accessor, returns a copy or reference to internal state without changing it. Marking a getter as a const member function promises it will not modify the object and allows calls on const objects. A setter, or mutator, takes input and updates internal state after validating the input. The validation enforces invariants — for example, refusing to set a temperature below absolute zero or a negative account balance. A common mistake is to expose a non-const getter that cannot be called on const objects, or to implement a setter that blindly trusts the caller. In the visual code panel you will see a TemperatureSensor example with a const getter and a setter that rejects unrealistic values. Read the code to see how the setter prints an error message when validation fails. When you write setters, consider whether to clamp invalid values, reject them, or throw an exception; choose based on the class contract and expected usage. How will your setter preserve the class's invariant?
